A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same federated-learning membership-inference research, despite retitling and substantial revision. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack comparisons on CIFAR100 and DermNet, experiments varying federated-learning factors, and defense evaluations, including supplementary AUC results.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and diffusion-model attack results, defense and sensitivity experiments, and generated-image examples, including appendix results.

M1.justification: The loss/cosine measurements, Gaussian modeling of non-target clients, and temporal aggregation remain, with Loss-III/Cos-III renamed FedMIA-I/II. v2 adds a 3-sigma filter before refitting the non-member distribution (Section 3.3, Equations 8–10) and explicitly thresholds averaged CDF scores. The filtering is a procedural refinement; the extensive reformulation does not establish an entirely new attack framework.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image classification on CIFAR100 and DermNet. v2 retains this coverage and adds latent-diffusion image generation on Tiny-ImageNet and CIFAR100 through FedEmbedding, substantially extending the task and exchanged-information settings actually evaluated.

E2.justification: The main attack baselines largely match after renaming. However, v2 adds Blackbox-Loss and Grad-Cosine to the defense comparisons and four baselines to the Non-IID comparison, where v1 Table 3 reported only Cos-III. Defense comparisons add augmentation, sampling, and their combination; quantization disappears from reported comparisons despite remaining described in the appendix.

E3.justification: Reported TPR evaluation changes from FPR=1% to 0.1%. The Non-IID grid changes from beta values 100, 5, 0.5, 0.1 to 10, 1, 0.1, and client/sample sweeps expand. Added generative experiments introduce FedEmbedding, a ten-class subset, and a 20-round Adam configuration in Table 3. These are revised or newly introduced reported protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds member/non-member score-distribution analysis (Figure 1) and an original-versus-generated-image case study (Figure 3). Defense and Non-IID robustness analyses expand, while the four existing federated-factor sweeps are revised. v1 Appendix B's AUC sensitivity plots and accompanying analysis are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.1 states that experiments are repeated more than three times; v2 omits this information. Both main result tables retain paired numerical entries, although v2 uses unexplained '+' notation instead of '±'. This weakens statistical reporting without establishing that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. AlexNet/CIFAR100 Cos-III reports 34.00% TPR at FPR=1% in v1 Table 2; FedMIA-II reports 66.98% at FPR=0.1% in v2 Table 1, which is not a same-setting gain. New diffusion rows report FedMIA-II TPRs of 4.50% on Tiny-ImageNet and 3.0% on CIFAR100. Rankings also change: Loss-Series leads AlexNet/DermNet AUC at 0.94, above both FedMIA variants.

T1.justification: v2 replaces v1's Boole-inequality/family-wise-error argument with an explicit likelihood-ratio and one-tailed formulation. It adds Theorem 1 on inclusion of average-threshold membership decisions within the union of per-round decisions, with a new Appendix C proof. The argument guaranteeing at least K−2 non-member non-target updates is also new. The appendix hypervolume definition is retained.

C1.justification: v1 centers on evaluating attack trends and recommending data-replacement defenses. v2 makes FedMIA's hypothesis-test formulation, theoretical justification, compatibility with existing measurements, and robustness the central contributions. Its effectiveness claims now extend to generative tasks and two federated structures; defense recommendation is no longer a principal abstract/conclusion contribution.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's explanation that heterogeneous clients weaken non-target shadow modeling and emphasizes Non-IID robustness. Defense interpretation shifts from favoring Mixup to favoring augmentation plus sampling, and generated-image similarity is newly interpreted as evidence of training-data membership. v2 Section 4.3 also reverses the stated hypervolume direction when claiming FedMIA-I superiority, contradicting Table 2.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds the member/non-member sampling recipe, IID allocation instructions, GPU assignments, explicit defense parameter ranges, and diffusion-training hyperparameters. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's training table and general defense descriptions. Most retained classifier training values and the code-access link remain unchanged; newly disclosed details do not establish changes to the original implementation.

R1.justification: The core FL/MIA related-work discussion remains. v2 adds discussion of source inference and privacy-defense auditing, newer FL attack citations, and references supporting diffusion, augmentation, and sampling; several earlier defense references are removed. The contrast with auxiliary-data shadow-model attacks receives greater emphasis, but this motivation already appears in v1 Section 3.4.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around FedMIA. The method narrative changes from an attack taxonomy to a hypothesis-test-first presentation. Separate defense sections are integrated into experimental robustness, with defense descriptions moved to the appendix. These constitute substantial rewriting and narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the introductory bar chart with score histograms and adds a workflow diagram, algorithm box, and generated-image panels. The main results table is transposed and expanded; the Non-IID table becomes multiple bar plots. Defense plots expand from six to twelve panels and move to the appendix, accompanied by a new main-text hypervolume table.

improvement.justification: v2 improves implementation documentation through Algorithm 1 and Appendix A and broadens empirical evidence to generation and additional defenses. These gains coexist with reduced repeat-count disclosure and contradictions affecting its superiority claims. Section 4.2 misattributes Table 1 scores, while Section 4.3 calls FedMIA-I's Mixup hypervolume 0.3609 better than 0.3328/0.3554 despite defining smaller values as stronger attacks. The expanded evidence has value, but these interpretation problems prevent a reliable net judgment of overall quality.
